data.title: Kroger launches a rewards Mastercard
data.description:
Grocery giant Kroger announced the launch of the Kroger Rewards World Elite Mastercard. The new co-branded credit card was built with the fintech company Imprint and Mastercard.

The card is designed to offer shoppers points at a rate of 5X their purchases, according to Kroger. Those purchases can be made through Kroger.com and the Kroger app.

In addition, the card fits within Kroger’s existing loyalty ecosystem. There, it will offer tiered rewards for fuel, in-store purchases, dining, and travel, plus a $100 welcome bonus.

Kroger’s leadership highlighted the company’s central ambitions when announcing the card.

Why Kroger is using the new Mastercard

“At Kroger, we’re always looking for new ways to help customers save,” said Megan Shaffer, group vice president of customer growth and strategy at Kroger. “From weekly grocery trips to filling up at the pump or paying bills, the Kroger Rewards World Elite Mastercard turns purchases into real savings. It is one more way we’re rewarding customers for the shopping they’re already doing.”

Imprint, the fintech platform powering the card’s technology, echoed the card’s diverse use.

“Kroger is one of America’s most trusted brands, with customer relationships built over decades of everyday shopping,” said Daragh Murphy, co-founder and CEO of Imprint. “Together, we set out to turn that loyalty into a card customers reach for every day, one that rewards the weekly Kroger trip and everything in between, with the modern, seamless experience they expect.”

Kroger ranks No. 7 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database. The database ranks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales. Kroger is also No. 1 in the database’s Food & Beverage category. It also competes with Mass Merchants — Walmart and Target — that rank higher in the Top 2000 for online grocery sales.

The new card’s role for Kroger

Kiki Del Valle, executive vice president in charge of U.S. market development at Mastercard, expects the card to help remove friction from the buying process.

“Grocery spending is one of the most consistent and essential parts of life,” she assessed. “Together with Kroger and Imprint, we’ve created a seamless rewards experience that helps shoppers earn more on the purchases they already make, turning regular grocery trips into meaningful savings.”

Serhii Nikolaichuk, founder and CEO of The Capital Index, a technology development studio based in Austin, Texas, sees the card providing additional value to Kroger.

“This isn’t a credit card,” Nikolaichuk said. “It’s a delivery app with a bank attached.”

Nikolaichuk noted the richest point tiers are reserved for Kroger.com and app purchases up to 5X. That compares with up to 3X in-store. Combined with a free Boost delivery membership built into the Kroger app, the total offerings send a clear signal.

“Kroger is paying shoppers to move from the aisle to the screen, where it can see every basket and plan the next one.”

That shift is also the real story behind the fintech partnership, he said. With Imprint running the card and a bank issuing it behind the scenes, Kroger, not a big bank, owns the relationship. It will also control the data and the customer experience. The bank becomes plumbing. Amazon and Target already proved to grocers that the card can function as the loyalty program; now, Nikolaichuk said, that card lives inside the grocer’s own app.

“The bigger reason is coming next: AI shopping assistants,” Nikolaichuk said. “When an assistant builds the weekly cart, it will pay with whatever card is already on file, and it will follow the points.”

The grocer that owns the app, the card and the data owns the default, he said. In his view, the real prize is not the next swipe, but the next year of automatic reorders.

Kroger’s grocery competition

As for how Kroger’s approach stacks up against the approaches of its competitors, Nikolaichuk said Amazon and Target have trained shoppers to expect roughly 5% back. In that context, Kroger’s 5X sounds comparable on its face. But the points, Nikolaichuk says, are only as good as what they buy — fuel and groceries inside Kroger’s own ecosystem. For a loyal Kroger household that already fills up at Kroger gas stations, he said, that can beat a general cash-back card. However, for anyone who shops around, simple cash back may remain more straightforward.

“Kroger isn’t buying loyalty at the checkout,” he added. “It’s buying the default for the day an AI agent does the shopping.”

Still, Francesco Onorato, director of growth at Brandmovers, a loyalty and promotions marketing company, noted that Kroger is making a smart move by connecting its new store credit card with its loyalty program. He sees a key question in whether or not that will be enough in today’s competitive grocery and retail market.

“What’s interesting is that Kroger is focusing high-value incentives on orders made through the app and including free delivery as part of the offer,” Onorato posited. “This strategy uses payments as a means of guiding shoppers out of the aisles and into the digital channels. A reliable, engaging and personalized online shopping experience is going to be the true test of how their bet will pay off.”

data.title: How Angara prepares for the Cyber 5, shifting consumer behavior
data.description:
Online-only jewelry retailer Angara has been preparing for the Cyber 5 by increasing its focus on flexibility, according to co-founder and CEO Ankur Daga.

That means giving its customers more choices and using data to respond faster to consumer behaviors. It also means “removing friction between inspiration and purchase,” Daga told Digital Commerce 360.

The Cyber 5 refers to the five-day period of Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday. And in 2025, the holiday shopping season taught Angara that “the companies that can listen and adapt in real time have a very different advantage from those trying to predict the customer months ahead,” he explained.

Among the retailer’s biggest lessons from 2025’s peak season was learning just how quickly consumer preferences can change in such periods, he said. In the jewelry space, a traditional retailer could be making inventory decisions for the holidays about five or six months in advance. But by the time retailers know what consumers want, it can be too late to react, he added.

“For us, that reinforced the importance of staying as close to real-time demand as possible,” Daga said. “Because we manufacture just in time, we’re not sitting on large amounts of finished inventory. We can see what customers are responding to — whether that’s a particular gemstone, shape, metal or price point — and adjust very quickly.”

Angara is No. 363 in the Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Angara is also No. 192 in Digital Commerce 360’s new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Angara’s approach leading up to the Cyber 5

Daga said Angara’s busiest periods are the holiday season and Valentine’s Day. Both also overlap with a “major engagement season.”

“From a business standpoint, our model is built to respond to demand in real time rather than forecasting it months in advance,” Daga said. “Because we own our entire supply chain, we’re able to adjust and produce as we see what customers are actually buying. During peak periods, preparation is as much about manufacturing capacity, technology and redundancy as it is about inventory.”

Daga said the Cyber 5 is an opportunity for Angara to ensure its ecommerce and manufacturing systems “can flex with demand.” The retailer’s holiday data indicates that its customers behave differently during the period.

The share of lab-grown gemstone sales increases, as does the share of stones above one carat. Stone shapes like the oval and emerald cut become more prominent.

“At the same time, the broader consumer environment is increasingly K-shaped, so we need to be prepared for shoppers trading up as well as those looking for greater value,” Daga said. “That means having the right mix of gemstones and diamonds available across sizes and qualities, sufficient manufacturing capacity and redundancy, and an ecommerce experience that makes it easy for customers to understand their options.”

He said Angara’s just-in-time model “is particularly valuable during the Cyber 5” because the retailer can watch demand develop and then adapt production around what customers are choosing.

How Angara improves its KPIs

Daga said Angara’s most effective strategy for improving its conversion rate and average order value (AOV) has been giving its customers more choices. At the same time, though, it has to make those choices easier to navigate.

“Jewelry is an incredibly personal purchase, so rather than pushing everyone toward a single product or price point, we allow customers to customize across metals, gemstones, stone quality and natural or lab-grown options,” Daga said. “That creates various options around a design and lets a customer trade up — or down — based on what matters most to them.”

Angara is also investing in richer product-page content and education. Daga explained that that’s because jewelry customers tend to do “a great deal” of research before completing their purchases.

Partially as a result of those refinements, Angara has seen a 500% year-over-year increase in traffic from its top three artificial intelligence (AI) referral sources, according to Daga.

“What we try not to do is optimize conversion simply by reducing quality or taking material out of a piece to reach an arbitrary price point,” Daga said. “Particularly with fine jewelry, there is a point at which making something lighter or thinner changes how it feels and wears.”

He noted that Angara would prefer to create value for consumers through aspects such as gemstone size, material or customization rather than compromise on a product’s quality.

data.title: DoorDash prepares nationwide Returns service, welcomes new retailers to marketplace
data.description:
DoorDash unveiled its new service for returns, along with other new app features and retail partners using its marketplace on Sept. 29 at its Dash Forward event in San Francisco.

The last-mile delivery app, which recently added Costco deliveries in the U.S. and joined Lowe’s and Wing to pilot drone delivery, also showed off its own DoorDash Air drone at the event — though Air was announced for early use with its food delivery partners Chipotle and Popeyes.

DoorDash CEO and co-founder Tony Xu appeared on stage to discuss the company’s latest moves. Xu was joined by other DoorDash executives, as well as representatives from Macy’s, Chipotle and Popeyes.

Dasher Returns is currently launching in a limited number of cities, with a nationwide rollout planned for November, according to DoorDash.

How will DoorDash’s Dasher Returns work?

“Starting today, we’re launching Dasher Returns,” said Shanna Prevé, chief revenue officer at DoorDash. “For a flat fee, DoorDash will come to your home, pick up your return, and take it back to the store for you.” 

Prevé walked through a use case with an order from Gap as an example, demonstrating that a return request can be placed right away or scheduled. After someone accepts the request, they pick up the item and take it back to the merchant’s physical store.

“Because that inventory goes back on the shelves today, Gap has a chance to resell it to another mom, and I get my refund in days, not weeks,” she stated.

Prevé called the experience “the return experience I wish I always had.” The company expects to make 80% of the retail orders it handles eligible for Dasher Returns by the end of 2026.

New retailers in the DoorDash app

DoorDash operates its own marketplace within its app for retailers, whose products are searchable and often available for same-day delivery.

“There are more than 200,000 retailers and grocers available across Deliveroo, DoorDash and Bolt,” Prevé shared, naming two of DoorDash’s other platforms. “Every single one of these retailers has decided a customer shouldn’t have to choose between getting something fast and getting it from a brand they trust.”

The company named five new brands set to appear in the app.

“Today, we are adding to that list of brands with some of my favorites, including Anthropologie, North Face, Timberland, Vans and Macy’s,” she said.

Prevé welcomed Josh Janos, vice president of marketplaces and digital partnerships at Macy’s, to the stage, to discuss the department store’s decision to sell through DoorDash. Macy’s previously began working with DoorDash as a white-label same-day and next-day fulfillment service in 2020, using it for orders made through Macys.com, Macy’s mobile app and Bloomingdales.com.

“Now, today we are announcing that the Macy’s catalog will be available from within the DoorDash Marketplace app,” Janos said.

Together, the companies also announced that DoorDash would be participating in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on Nov. 26 in New York City.

Macy’s ranks No. 17 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database. The market research tool ranks the largest North American online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

AI tools and drone delivery

In addition to Dasher Returns, DoorDash detailed other new launches for customers and delivery workers on its platform. Those included:

  • DoorDash MCP for corporate ordering, connecting AI agents to DoorDash’s system
  • Text DoorDash, a system for ordering from DoorDash through text messages, currently open to users through a waitlist
  • Ask DoorDash, a conversational interface for shoppers
  • DashBuddy, a text-based SMS chatbot for delivery workers, which it refers to as Dashers, using the platform
  • DoorDash Air, which is entering use for some Chipotle and Popeyes food orders

Last, Stanley Tang, chief product officer and co-founder at DoorDash, offered an update on the company’s Dot delivery robots. The wheeled units debuted a year ago and have since continued to increase workloads. The robots currently traverse roads, bike lanes and sidewalks to complete orders.

“Today, Dot is scaling, making deliveries for over 2,000 store locations across Greater Phoenix, from local restaurants — like Grove and Real Cafe — to national chains like Little Caesars,” Tang said. “Each Dot is completing three times the number of deliveries compared to last year.”

data.title: Ikea, Kodiak prepare to launch driverless freight service in Texas
data.description:
After four years of testing autonomous freight with a safety driver behind the wheel, Ikea is preparing to go fully driverless in Texas using Kodiak’s autonomous driving technology.

Later this year, the Sweden-based home furnishings retailer plans to launch driverless service with Kodiak on a roughly 220-mile stretch connecting the Houston and Dallas metro areas. The highway leg is part of a nearly 300-mile delivery route moving Ikea goods from its Baytown distribution center to its store in Frisco.

“IKEA has been a wonderful partner and customer for four years, and this represents the next chapter,” Don Burnette, Kodiak’s founder and CEO, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Sept. 29.

Originally intended as a three-month trial, the pilot between Ikea and Kodiak continued for four years. During that span, Kodiak said its trucks carried more than 1,300 Ikea loads and logged more than 750,000 autonomous miles. The company described the service as operating “without incident” and with a “nearly perfect” on-time delivery record.

The launch comes as autonomous freight moves beyond small-scale pilots and into day-to-day operations. Walmart, Kroger and Loblaw have all tested or deployed autonomous vehicles for middle-mile deliveries, while PepsiCo said it’s expanding driverless freight across several states.

Ikea ranks No. 6 in the Europe Database, Digital Commerce 360’s ranking of the largest online retailers in the region by their annual ecommerce sales. There, Digital Commerce 360 categorizes it as a Housewares & Home Furnishings retailer.

How Kodiak is preparing for driverless freight

In a Sept. 29 update, Kodiak said it has hauled Ikea goods along the Texas route day and night, seven days a week, and through varying weather conditions. Later this year, Ikea will become Kodiak’s launch shipper for driverless long-haul highway service, with no safety driver aboard.

Kodiak provides the autonomous driving system behind the trucks. Its core product, the Kodiak Driver, combines AI-powered software with modular hardware installed on commercial vehicles. The company offers the technology through a Driver-as-a-Service model and strategic partnerships.

Before it removes safety drivers, Kodiak is also completing its final round of testing. In a Sept. 25 release, the company shared that its trucks have been making deliveries between its Lancaster, Texas, hub and Houston since August without the driver taking control, including on surface streets. Kodiak said it’s also running closed-course tests to recreate situations “that occur too rarely, or are too risky, to test on public highways.”

“Our progress since beginning our final push towards driverless commercial deliveries has been incredible, and it is a strong signal we are ready to scale unsupervised driverless service on long-haul lanes,” Burnette said in the Sept. 25 release.

Kodiak already operates without drivers in another setting. Since December 2024, Atlas Energy Solutions has used customer-owned trucks equipped with the Kodiak Driver to haul freight in the Permian Basin of West Texas and eastern New Mexico. As of June, Kodiak reported that 35 Atlas trucks using the system had logged more than 40,000 hours of paid driverless operations.

What driverless freight could mean for Ikea

With Ikea, Kodiak is taking that technology from an industrial setting to a major interstate freight lane. The company said four years of testing also taught it how to integrate autonomous trucks into Ikea’s supply chain, from scheduling departures and unloading docks to using vehicle data for predictive maintenance.

“We now know exactly what it takes to transform the underlying technology into an AI-driven product that generates value and efficiency,” Kodiak said in its Sept. 29 blog post.

Ikea has already seen some of those potential benefits elsewhere. After testing, Ikea China permanently adopted self-driving electric vehicles at its Hefei operation, Ingka Group said in March. Ingka is Ikea’s largest franchisee and operates its U.S. retail business, including 61 retail locations.

The vehicles move goods between a warehouse and the store for customer pickup orders and restocking. During the test, the trucks traveled nearly 75,600 kilometers, or about 47,000 miles, according to Ingka. The company said they cut average wait times for pickup orders from six hours to two. Transportation costs between Ikea locations also fell by more than 50%.

Ikea is also testing autonomous deliveries directly to customers in China. Ingka said it is evaluating whether the Hefei model could work in other markets where regulations and infrastructure allow.

Other companies expand driverless freight

Retailers and consumer brands are increasingly using autonomous trucks for middle-mile routes.

Walmart was an early adopter. In 2021, the retailer and autonomous trucking company Gatik removed the safety driver from box trucks running a roughly 7-mile route between a Walmart facility and a neighborhood market in Bentonville, Arkansas. According to Gatik, it was “the first time an autonomous trucking company has removed the safety driver from a commercial delivery route on the middle mile.”

More recently, in June, PepsiCo signed a multiyear agreement with Gatik to expand autonomous freight across its North American supply chain. Driverless trucks are already operating for PepsiCo in Texas, Arizona and Arkansas. FreightWaves reported that the network serves about 250 retail locations, including Walmart and Dollar General stores. Walmart ranks No. 2 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales. Dollar General is ranked No. 674 in the Top 1000.

Meanwhile, the economics of autonomous trucking may depend heavily on distance and scale. A 2026 study by researchers at North Dakota State University estimated potential savings of about 13% for a 200-mile hub-to-hub route, rising to 31% at 1,000 miles when fleets reach sufficient scale.

Without that scale, shorter autonomous routes could cost more, they found. The study did not examine Ikea, but its roughly 220-mile driverless leg is close to the shorter route modeled.

data.title: Amazon brings back Prime Big Deal Days in first week of October
data.description:
Amazon is bringing back its Prime Big Deal Days promotion, its sales event in October, continuing its recent approach of holding a sale in spring, summer and fall.

Like the summer iteration of the event, both Prime Day and Prime Big Deal Days are member-exclusive promotions. Amazon is offering early deals ahead of Prime Big Deal Days. Those include discounts on Amazon devices, Kindle, Amazon Music Unlimited and Amazon Haul.

Amazon Haul is the merchant’s storefront for budget-conscious consumers, focusing on ultra-low prices. The marketplace launched that storefront in beta in November 2024 as a competitor to Shein and Temu.

“Once fall arrives, there’s so much to get ready for — the hosting, the decorating, the holiday gifting — and Prime Big Deal Days makes it easy to check it all off while saving,” said Carmen Nestares, vice president of North America Marketing and Prime Tech, in an announcement.

For the first two years, in 2015 and 2026, Amazon Prime Day was exclusively a 24-hour sales event during the summer. From 2017 through 2024, it was a two-day event. Last year, it ran for four days, and Amazon has planned the same length for summer 2026.

Amazon ranks No. 1 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database. The database is how Digital Commerce 360 tracks the largest North American online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Amazon is also No. 3 in Digital Commerce 360’s Global Online Marketplaces Database. That database ranks the 100 largest such marketplaces by third-party gross merchandise value (GMV).

When is Amazon Prime Day 2026?

In 2026, the Amazon Prime Big Deal Days event will run 48 hours, between Oct. 6 and 7. That’s nearly the same time frame as in 2025, when the event ran Oct. 7 and 8.

This year’s Prime Big Deal Days event will feature new product drops three times a day, according to Amazon:

  • Midnight PDT
  • 8 a.m.
  • 1 p.m.

Amazon said brands including Shark, Princess Polly and Soundcore will participate in the drops.

Amazon said members can find deals on Halloween products, for game-day and fall hosting, as well as for holiday gifting. It gave examples of costumes and accessories for as low as $5, candy for less than $10, charcuterie boards, slow cookers and a list of top toys.

Members can use Alexa for Shopping to set up deal and price alerts, as well as for auto-buying. Shoppers can also check price history on products or ask Alexa for Shopping to see up to 365 days of pricing insights.

Amazon released Alexa for Shopping in mid-May 2026. It serves as an artificial intelligence (AI) agent that combines Amazon’s Rufus and Alexa+ offerings. In June, Amazon added customized product designs within Alexa for Shopping, for certain merchandise.

During the summer, the Amazon Prime Day sales event ran for four days, from June 23 through June 26. That was just the second time that Amazon held its main Prime Day event of the year in June, as the retailer has most often opted for July.

The last time it made that decision was in 2021. Aside from that year and 2020 — when the COVID-19 pandemic shifted summer strategies — the summer iterations of the Amazon Prime Day event have always been in the middle of July. 

Prior to that, its most recent Prime Day-equivalent, Big Spring Sale, ran at the end of March 2026. It lasted for one week, from March 25 through 31.

 


How much did Amazon make on Prime Day?

Although Amazon did not attach a dollar amount to its summer 2026 Prime Day sales, it said the event was its biggest ever.

Digital Commerce 360 previously reported that during the time frame of the summer Prime Day event, U.S. ecommerce sales outside of Amazon reached $26.4 billion. That outdid Prime Day 2025’s impact, generating $24.1 billion in nationwide ecommerce sales.

As a comparison point, U.S. consumers spent $32.45 billion online across Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday  in 2025. Those were three of the largest days of that year in terms of online retail sales.

How many countries will Prime Day take place in?

Amazon Prime Big Deal Days will take place in 22 countries:

  1. Austria
  2. Belgium
  3. Canada
  4. Colombia
  5. Egypt
  6. France
  7. Germany
  8. Ireland
  9. Italy
  10. Luxembourg
  11. Mexico
  12. Netherlands
  13. Poland
  14. Portugal
  15. Saudi Arabia
  16. Singapore
  17. Spain
  18. Sweden
  19. Turkey
  20. United Arab Emirates
  21. United Kingdom
  22. United States

Amazon said Prime members in Australia, Brazil, India and Japan will be able to shop Prime Day deals later in the summer.

When is Amazon Prime Day usually?

Dates for Amazon Prime Day event in the past:

  • 12th: June 23-26, 2026
  • 11th: July 8-11, 2025
  • 10th: July 16-July 17, 2024
  • Ninth: July 11-12, 2023
  • Eighth: July 12-13, 2022
  • Seventh: June 21-22, 2021
  • Sixth: Oct 13-14, 2020
  • Fifth: July 15-16, 2019
  • Fourth: July 16-17, 2018
  • Third: July 11-12, 2017
  • Second: July 12, 2016
  • First: July 15, 2015

How often is Amazon Prime Day?

Until 2022, Amazon Prime Day was once a year in the summer. In 2022, the retail giant added another Prime Day event in October. So how many times a year is Prime Day? The answer used to be once. Amazon then established a two-year pattern of two separate sales events.

As of 2024, Amazon held its inaugural Big Spring Sale, from March 20 through 25. That Big Spring Sale event was open to all customers, and Prime members received access to exclusive deals, Amazon said.

Currently, the answer is that Amazon Prime Day — in its various sales event forms — is three times a year.

How do you sign up for a Prime membership?

You can join Prime or start a free trial at Amazon Prime Day. Amazon has recently faced a lawsuit from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission alleging the ecommerce giant duped consumers into signing up for its Prime membership service and deliberately made it hard to cancel. 

How to prepare to find deals on Prime Day 

The value of Prime Day to retailers both small and large is undisputed, as millions of shoppers visit the site in search of once-a-year deals.

  • Sign up for the Prime Insider newsletter to hear about Amazon Prime member benefits and find updates on deals and events.
  • Create deal alerts for recommendations. As an Amazon Prime Member, you can subscribe to receive deal alert notifications related to recent Amazon searches and recently viewed items. All you have to do is visit the Prime Day event page on the Amazon app before Prime Day to create deal alerts. Once Prime Day arrives, members will receive push notifications on any available deals.
  • Get deal notifications from Alexa. Alexa can make sure you don’t miss any Amazon deals. Members can add products to their Wish List, Cart, or Save for Later, and then ask Alexa to notify them about the deal.
  • Set a reminder so you don’t miss the multi-day event.
  • Check back here to see the latest updates.

What are the Big Spring Sale and Big Deal Days, and how are they different from Prime Days?

Amazon called its inaugural March promotional period its Big Spring Sale. In October 2023, it created a new fall sale event called Big Deal Days. Amazon’s Big Spring Sale is not exclusive to Prime members. The online retailer also held a fall sale in 2022 for the first time, called the Early Access Sale.

Prime Day is now Amazon’s biggest sale of the year. It is usually held during the summer months. In 2025, it was July 8 through July 11. Historically, the annual event has been two days and for Prime members only. 

Prime Day, which features deals on many products on Amazon.com, began in 2015 as a celebration of Amazon’s 20th year in business. It turned into a summer sales holiday to drum up additional business for Amazon — and the retailer’s marketplace sellers — before the holiday shopping season. In recent years, other large retailers have offered promotions on their own websites around Prime Day to take advantage of the additional online shoppers.

Abbas Haleem, Brian Warmoth, Mary Meisenzahl, James Risley and Paul Conley contributed to this report.
